title: Marsh: Global Commercial Insurance Rates Fall About 5% in Q3 2026, the Ninth Straight Decline, While US Casualty Is the Only Line Still Rising
summary: Marsh's Q3 2026 index shows global commercial insurance rates down about 5% (after 6% in Q2), with property down 10%, cyber down 4% and US casualty up 6%, while CRC Group reports US property renewals still down about 11% but with the pace of decline moderating.
description:
The insurance buyer's market has now lasted nine consecutive quarters. Marsh's Global Insurance Market Index, reported by Reinsurance News on October 21, 2026, shows that global commercial insurance rates fell about 5% in the third quarter of 2026, following a 6% decline in the second quarter. It is the ninth straight quarterly decrease. The index tracks the change in premiums on renewing commercial policies that Marsh places for clients, so it reflects what buyers actually paid compared with a year earlier.

The line-by-line picture shows a market that is softening unevenly. Global property rates fell 10% in the third quarter, after falling 12% in the second quarter and 9% in the first. Casualty, which covers liability risks, rose 1% globally, slower than the 2% rise in the second quarter. The United States was the only region with rising casualty rates, at 6% compared with 7% in the second quarter. Financial and professional lines, which include directors and officers and professional indemnity, fell 3% globally, extending a decline that Marsh counts at 17 consecutive quarters, while US rates in that line rose 1%, unchanged from the previous quarter. Cyber rates fell 4% globally, the 13th consecutive quarterly decline and the same pace as in the second quarter, though US cyber rates stabilised.

The regional composite figures are: India, the Middle East and Africa down 14%; the Pacific down 12%; Latin America and the Caribbean down 9%; the United Kingdom down 8%; Canada, Europe and Asia each down 6%; and the United States down 1%, compared with a 2% decline in the second quarter. Property rates fell fastest in India, the Middle East and Africa (15%), the Pacific (14%) and Latin America and the Caribbean (13%), followed by the UK (11%), the US (10%), Europe (9%), Canada (8%) and Asia (7%).

Marsh attributes the declines to competition among insurers, abundant capacity and favourable reinsurance costs. John Donnelly, president of global placement at Marsh Risk, said that "geopolitical uncertainty and broader economic concerns remain part of the operating environment." The reference to the environment is a reminder that pricing is only one part of a buyer's decision. Terms, deductibles and exclusions also matter, and insurers have been competing on those too.

A second data source points the same way but suggests the slide is flattening. CRC Group, a large wholesale broker, reported on October 21 that its Property REDY Index, which tracks renewal pricing on property accounts, showed year-over-year changes of minus 12.0% in July, minus 11.4% in August and minus 11.1% in September 2026. That compares with minus 12.8% in June and minus 13.3% in May, so the declines are becoming smaller. A year earlier, the same months showed much smaller falls, of 6.0% in July, 5.2% in August and 7.0% in September 2025, which shows how far prices have dropped since. Roughly 91% to 93% of CRC's property accounts renewed flat or at reduced rates in the third quarter of 2026, while accounts facing increases of 10% or more made up less than 2% of the book. CRC says ample reinsurance and insurance capacity supports competitive conditions, carriers are prioritising profitable accounts, and competition is strongest for accounts with good loss histories and strong underwriting information. It expects the market to remain favourable for buyers, with the softening pace potentially levelling off heading into 2027. CRC's data cover its own book and do not give regional or excess and surplus lines breakdowns.

The most pointed warning comes from the industry itself. Evan Greenberg, chairman and chief executive of Chubb, was quoted by Reinsurance News on October 21 describing "a lot of hungry and extremely naive capacity available." He said pricing is becoming more aggressive in the United States and London, that competition in property is the first sign of softening, and that softer conditions are spreading into more casualty lines, where pricing in many areas is not keeping up with loss costs. Loss costs, he said, are steady but still well above general inflation. He credited Chubb's diversification across countries and lines of business for leaving it relatively well positioned. The article does not quantify specific price declines and the remarks are as reported, not a transcript.

Those comments matter because they describe a risk rather than a result. Chubb's own third-quarter results, reported on October 20, showed a P&C combined ratio of 84.1% and nine-month P&C underwriting income of $5.79 billion, up 33.7%, so the company is profitable. A profitable insurer warning about competitors' pricing is a classic late-cycle signal: when capacity keeps arriving and prices keep falling, underwriting margins eventually narrow, and insurers that cut prices below the cost of claims can face losses later.

What should buyers do with this? In property, where rates are down 10% globally and 11% in US renewals, buyers can use competition to seek better terms, broader cover and lower deductibles, but there is a risk in choosing the cheapest option from a carrier that may not be disciplined; the financial strength and claims record of the insurer matter. In US casualty, where rates are still rising 6%, the softening has not arrived, and buyers should prepare for continued increases, particularly for lines with large liability exposures. In cyber, twelve consecutive quarters of declines mean prices are far below their peak, but cyber losses can be sudden and correlated, so coverage terms deserve attention.

For insurers, the next quarters will test discipline. Lower reinsurance costs, expected to fall further at the January 1 renewals, give them room to cut prices, but exceptionally light catastrophe losses in 2026, which Gallagher Re puts at the lowest for a nine-month period since 2019, have helped profits. A change in catastrophe experience could alter the picture quickly.

Two caveats apply. The Marsh figures come from a secondary report of its release and were not checked against Marsh's own page, which could not be loaded. And an index of renewal changes measures price, not the total spent by any one business, which also depends on its exposures, claims history and the risk it chooses to retain.
source_name: Reinsurance News (Marsh Global Insurance Market Index, Q3 2026, Oct 21, 2026) and CRC Group Q3 2026 Property REDY Index
image_alt: Insurance documents and calculator representing commercial insurance pricing (illustrative)
key_points: Marsh says global commercial insurance rates fell about 5% in Q3 2026, the ninth straight quarterly decline, after a 6% drop in Q2.
Property rates fell 10% globally (after 12% in Q2), casualty rose 1% (US +6%, down from 7%), financial and professional lines fell 3% and cyber fell 4%, the 13th consecutive decline.
By region the composite fell 14% in India, the Middle East and Africa, 12% in the Pacific, 9% in Latin America, 8% in the UK, 6% in Canada, Europe and Asia, and 1% in the US.
CRC Group reports US property renewals down 12.0% in July, 11.4% in August and 11.1% in September, with roughly 91% to 93% of accounts renewing flat or lower and the pace of decline moderating.
Chubb's Evan Greenberg described 'a lot of hungry and extremely naive capacity' and said softer conditions are spreading into more casualty lines where pricing is not keeping up with loss costs.
why_it_matters: Businesses of every size are still enjoying lower insurance prices, but the pace of decline is slowing and one of the industry's most experienced executives is warning about undisciplined capacity. That combination is what usually precedes a change in the insurance cycle.

title: Global Insured Catastrophe Losses Hit $92 Billion in the First Nine Months of 2026, 29% Below Average and the Lowest Since 2019, Gallagher Re Says
summary: Gallagher Re puts global insured natural-catastrophe losses for January to September 2026 at $92 billion, 29% below the 10-year average of $128 billion; severe convective storms caused almost 60% of the total, and no single event exceeded $10 billion for six straight quarters.
description:
Insurers and reinsurers have enjoyed an unusually light year for natural-catastrophe claims. Gallagher Re, the reinsurance broking arm of Arthur J. Gallagher, reported on October 21, 2026 that global insured losses from natural disasters totalled $92 billion in the first nine months of 2026. That is the lowest figure for the January to September period since 2019 and about 29% below the 10-year average of $128 billion. Insured losses are the amount paid or expected to be paid by insurers, as distinct from the total economic cost of disasters, which includes uninsured damage.

The most striking feature of the data is the absence of a single very large event. Gallagher Re says six consecutive quarters have passed without any natural catastrophe producing more than $10 billion in insured losses. That does not mean disasters were rare. The firm recorded 54 events with economic losses of at least $1 billion, and 24 events with insured losses of at least $1 billion. The year's losses came from many mid-sized events rather than from one headline catastrophe.

Severe convective storms, the category that includes hail, tornadoes and thunderstorm winds, dominated. In the United States, they caused at least $43 billion in insured losses, the fourth straight year above $40 billion. In Europe, they caused at least $9 billion, including $3.8 billion from a late-August outbreak. Globally, severe convective storms accounted for almost 60% of insured natural-catastrophe losses in the period. This is a persistent theme: although hurricanes and earthquakes produce the largest single-event losses, repeated hail and wind events add up. The PERILS estimate for the July European storms, which reached €2.8 billion, and Canadian Prairie hail losses of $923 million fit the same pattern.

The report also names a hurricane that falls outside the period. Hurricane Isaias reached Florida's Panhandle on October 9 as a Category 2 storm. Because it happened after the end of September, it is not in the $92 billion figure, and Gallagher Re expects its insured losses to be in the low to mid-single-digit billions of dollars. Separately, the report mentions Hurricane Lala, which passed near Hawaii's Big Island in mid-August and produced economic losses above $1 billion, the state's second such weather disaster of the year.

Climate conditions provide context. According to Gallagher Re, global temperatures for the first nine months of 2026 were the second highest on record, and France, the United Kingdom and the contiguous United States each had their warmest June-to-August period on record. The article cites a greater than 81% probability from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration that El Niño stays "very strong" into January 2027, with a later shift towards La Niña also possible. These are forecasts of climate patterns, not of losses, and the source does not link them to specific loss expectations.

Steve Bowen, Gallagher Re's chief science officer, offered a caution in a quote reported with the findings: "catastrophe activity and catastrophe losses are not necessarily the same thing." The point is that the number and intensity of events can be high without producing high insured losses if they occur in sparsely populated or well-protected places, or fail to strike major cities. The reverse is also true: a single storm landing on a dense, high-value area can generate large losses.

The financial effects are visible across the industry. Reinsurers have reported strong profits: Munich Re's second-quarter major losses were EUR 191 million, far below the level it plans for, and Chubb's nine-month P&C underwriting income reached a record $5.79 billion. Light losses also add to the capital of reinsurers and alternative-capital investors, which supports the downward pressure on prices at the January 1 renewals. Marsh's index shows global commercial insurance rates falling for a ninth consecutive quarter, with property down 10% in the third quarter.

There is another side. Insured losses are only part of the story, and the source does not give an aggregate economic loss total or discuss the protection gap, the share of losses that are uninsured. Households and businesses in affected areas can still suffer severe damage even in a year with low insured totals. Costs borne by governments and individuals do not appear in these figures. For homeowners, low industry-wide losses do not translate directly into lower premiums, particularly in states where rates have been rising to catch up with earlier losses.

How should one read the number? A total 29% below average is a good year for insurers, but not evidence that risk is declining. The ten-year average itself rose as losses climbed in the late 2010s and early 2020s. Insurers price for the long run, and they treat quiet years as part of the cycle. A season in which a major hurricane or earthquake strikes a populated area can add tens of billions of dollars in a few days.

The coming months matter. Hurricane Isaias, with its expected low to mid-single-digit billions, will add to the full-year tally, and the end of the Atlantic hurricane season on November 30 will show whether 2026 remains a light year. Gallagher Re's full-year report, usually published in January, will give the final number. In the meantime, the nine-month data explain why reinsurers are preparing for price cuts and why insurers argue that discipline is needed to avoid repeating past mistakes.
source_name: Reinsurance News and Claims Journal (Gallagher Re nine-month catastrophe report, Oct 21, 2026)
key_points: Gallagher Re estimates global insured natural-disaster losses at $92 billion for January to September 2026, the lowest nine-month total since 2019 and about 29% below the 10-year average of $128 billion.

Six consecutive quarters have passed without a single natural catastrophe causing more than $10 billion of insured losses; there were 54 events with economic losses of at least $1 billion and 24 with insured losses of at least $1 billion.
US severe convective storms caused at least $43 billion, the fourth straight year above $40 billion, and European storms at least $9 billion including $3.8 billion from a late-August outbreak.
Globally, severe convective storms caused almost 60% of insured natural-catastrophe losses; Hurricane Isaias hit Florida's Panhandle on October 9 and falls outside the period.

Steve Bowen, Gallagher Re's chief science officer, said 'catastrophe activity and catastrophe losses are not necessarily the same thing,' and global temperatures were the second highest on record for the period.
why_it_matters: Low catastrophe losses explain why insurers and reinsurers are highly profitable and why prices are falling. But the total was driven by the absence of a mega-event, not by calmer weather, so a single severe event could change the picture quickly.

title: Daiichi Life's Australian Arm Proposes to Buy the Rest of Challenger at A$11.80 a Share in a Non-Binding Offer
summary: TAL Dai-ichi Life Australia, a subsidiary of Japan's Daiichi Life Group, has made a non-binding indicative proposal to buy the remaining 79.5% of Challenger at A$11.80 per share through a scheme of arrangement, subject to due diligence, final terms and regulatory approvals.
description:
A Japanese-owned life insurer in Australia has made an approach to buy out one of the country's best-known annuity providers. Reinsurance News reported on October 22, 2026 that TAL Daiichi Life Australia Pty Limited, known as TDA and a subsidiary of Daiichi Life Group, has submitted a "non-binding indicative proposal" to the board of Challenger. The proposal would see TDA acquire the remaining 79.5% of Challenger's ordinary shares for A$11.80 per share, implemented through a scheme of arrangement.

A scheme of arrangement is a court-approved procedure commonly used for takeovers in Australia and the United Kingdom. Shareholders vote on the deal, and if enough support it and the court approves, the transfer binds all shareholders. It requires cooperation from the target's board, which is why an initial approach is usually made privately and described as an indicative proposal. "Non-binding" means neither side is committed: Challenger's board could reject it, negotiate a higher price or agree to engage.

The source, as available for this article, leaves out several details that matter. It does not state the premium that A$11.80 represents over Challenger's recent share price, so it is not possible to say how generous the offer is. It does not disclose an overall valuation, and it does not directly state how many Challenger shares TDA already owns. The reference to the "remaining 79.5%" implies TDA holds about 20.5%, but that is an inference from the arithmetic, not a statement in the report. No quote from executives or from Challenger's board is included, and the board's response has not been reported.

The proposal is conditional on three things: satisfactory exclusive due diligence, agreement of final terms, and all necessary regulatory approvals. Due diligence means TDA would examine Challenger's books in detail, and "exclusive" suggests it would ask for a period in which Challenger does not negotiate with others. Regulatory approvals in a deal like this would typically involve Australian authorities that supervise insurers and review foreign investment, but the source does not name them, and no timetable is given.

There is a history behind the approach. In April 2025, MS&AD Insurance Holdings, the Japanese non-life insurer, agreed to sell about 104,353,125 Challenger shares, equal to 15.1% of the company, to TDA for 80 billion yen. That transaction put the Daiichi subsidiary in a significant minority position. The 15.1% stake and the 79.5% remaining suggest that TDA holds roughly a fifth of Challenger after that and any earlier purchases, though, again, the exact current holding is not stated in the report.

Why would Daiichi Life want Challenger? The source does not give reasons, so the following is context and not reporting. Challenger specialises in annuities, products that convert a lump sum into a guaranteed income stream, and Australia has a large pool of retirement savings in its superannuation system, with a growing number of people moving from saving to spending in retirement. The Australian prudential regulator recently changed the capital rules for longevity products to make them easier to offer, so the market for lifetime income products is attracting attention. A Japanese life insurer with experience of an ageing society may see Australia as a market with similar needs.

The proposal also continues a pattern of Japanese life insurers expanding abroad. Sumitomo Life has set aside up to ¥1 trillion for deals in the United States and Southeast Asia, Meiji Yasuda completed its purchase of Legal & General's US business in February 2026, and Nippon Life has built stakes in Corebridge and Resolution Life. Daiichi, which has owned Protective Life in the United States since 2015, has been active in Australia through TAL. Fitch's recent review of Japanese insurers notes that overseas operations are a major source of earnings for the large groups.

What happens next? If Challenger's board is willing, it could grant TDA due diligence, and the parties could negotiate a binding scheme implementation deed, which would be announced with details of price, conditions and timetable. The board could also reject the proposal, in which case TDA could raise its offer, hold its stake or make a direct approach to shareholders, although none of these outcomes is reported. Shareholders, including large institutions, would need to vote, and the scheme would require approval by the court. Regulators would also need to review the effect on policyholders and on the stability of the annuity market.

For Challenger's annuity customers, nothing changes now. Their policies are contracts with Challenger's life company and remain in force whatever happens to the share register. A change of control, if it occurs, would be subject to regulatory review, which would consider the financial strength of the new owner and the protection of policyholders.

Readers should treat the report with caution. It is based on a single short announcement, with no price premium, valuation or board comment, and the proposal is explicitly non-binding. Many indicative proposals do not result in a completed deal. The key facts to watch are Challenger's response, any disclosure of TDA's current holding and any change in the price or terms.
image_alt: Business skyline representing a cross-border insurance takeover proposal (illustrative)
key_points: TAL Daiichi Life Australia Pty Limited, a subsidiary of Daiichi Life Group, submitted a non-binding indicative proposal to Challenger's board to acquire the remaining 79.5% of Challenger's ordinary shares.
The proposed price is A$11.80 per share, to be implemented through a scheme of arrangement; the source does not state a premium to the market price or an overall valuation.
The proposal depends on satisfactory exclusive due diligence, agreement of final terms and all required regulatory approvals, and no binding agreement has been reached.
In April 2025 MS&AD Insurance Holdings agreed to sell about 104.4 million Challenger shares, 15.1% of the company, to TAL Dai-ichi for 80 billion yen.
The source does not report Challenger's board response or give a timetable.
why_it_matters: Challenger is one of Australia's main providers of annuities, which turn retirement savings into guaranteed income. A full takeover by a Japanese life insurer would continue the trend of Japanese insurers buying growth abroad and could affect how retirement income products are supplied in Australia.

title: PERILS Raises Insured Loss Estimate for July's 'SCS Cerry' Storms in Germany, France, Switzerland and Italy to €2.8 Billion
summary: PERILS raised its insured loss estimate for the July 13-19, 2026 severe convective storms named SCS Cerry to €2,806 million from €2,186 million; the event hit Germany, France, Switzerland and Italy with large hail, damaging winds and heavy rain, and CatIQ lifted its estimate for September's southern Ontario storms to C$671 million.
description:
A mid-July run of thunderstorms across central Europe has turned out to be more expensive for insurers than first thought. PERILS, the independent provider of catastrophe loss data for Europe and other markets, reported on October 21, 2026 that it had raised its estimate of insured losses from the severe convective storms of July 13 to 19, 2026 to €2,806 million, or about €2.8 billion. Its initial estimate had been €2,186 million, so the figure has risen by about €620 million, or roughly 28%. The storm system was named "SCS Cerry" by the Free University of Berlin, which names weather systems in Europe, and the abbreviation SCS stands for severe convective storm.

The event affected four countries: Germany, France, Switzerland and Italy. According to PERILS, some of the storm cells produced very large hail, damaging wind gusts and intense rainfall. The estimate is based on loss data supplied by affected insurers and covers property and motor lines. Property includes damage to homes and commercial buildings; motor covers vehicles, which are often badly damaged by hail. PERILS does not provide a breakdown by country or line in the material reviewed here, so it is not possible to say how much of the €2.8 billion arose in Germany compared with the other three countries.

The pattern of upward revisions is common. The first estimate relies on early reports and market-share-based extrapolation, and later estimates draw on actual claims data as insurers inspect damage, settle claims and book costs. For hail, vehicle claims tend to be reported quickly while commercial property claims take longer, which means totals often keep rising for months. PERILS will publish a third estimate on January 19, 2027, six months after the end of the event. Readers should therefore treat the €2.8 billion as the latest estimate, not a final figure.

Quotes from the two organisations placed the storms in a wider context. Luzi Hitz of PERILS said: "severe convective storms are a major risk for the insurance markets in Europe and Canada." Caroline Floyd of CatIQ said: "The growing global impacts of this peril reaffirm the importance of having accurate data." CatIQ, a Toronto-based subsidiary of PERILS, publishes the industry loss estimates for Canada.

The same report updated a Canadian event. CatIQ raised its estimate for the severe convective storms that hit southern Ontario, including Toronto, on September 2 and 3, 2026 to C$671 million from C$563 million. As with the European event, the estimate covers property and motor lines. The next CatIQ update is due on December 3, 2026. The Ontario figure is an increase of C$108 million, or about 19%, from the previous estimate.

How does SCS Cerry compare with the year's other storm losses? Gallagher Re's nine-month catastrophe report, also published on October 21, estimates that severe convective storms in Europe caused at least $9 billion of insured losses between January and September 2026, including $3.8 billion from a late-August outbreak. The report treats the late-August event separately from SCS Cerry, and the sources reviewed here do not say how the July event ranks within the $9 billion. In the United States, severe convective storms caused at least $43 billion. Globally, they were almost 60% of insured natural-catastrophe losses in the nine months.

Why does this matter for ordinary customers? In Germany, home and contents insurance often includes cover for hail and storm, but the details vary by policy, and the insurance industry's data show that hail is a growing cause of damage. Motor insurance covers hail damage to cars under comprehensive cover. Repeated losses push up the cost of reinsurance for storm-exposed regions and can lead insurers to raise premiums or deductibles. At the same time, reinsurance markets are softening because of ample capital and light overall catastrophe losses, which may limit how quickly higher claims translate into higher prices.

For insurers, accurate estimates are important for reserving, for reinsurance recoveries and for deciding how much capacity to offer. Industry loss indices like those of PERILS are used by reinsurers and by investors in catastrophe bonds, where payouts can depend on the size of industry-wide losses, though the source does not say whether any such instrument is affected by this event.

Readers should also keep in mind what a loss estimate represents. PERILS compiles market-wide insured losses from data provided by participating insurers, so the figure is an industry total and not a measure of any one company's exposure. Insured losses exclude damage that was not covered, such as properties without storm or hail cover, and they exclude public-sector costs. Where cover is widespread, as with motor comprehensive policies in many European countries, insured losses capture more of the damage. Where cover is patchy, the insured figure understates the total harm. The source does not provide the corresponding economic loss, so the full cost to the four countries cannot be judged from this report.

What remains unknown? The report does not provide the number of claims, the sizes of hailstones or the insurers most affected. It does not break down losses by country. It also does not say whether further increases are expected. For those details, readers should consult the PERILS publication. The main takeaway is that the severe convective storm peril, which was once seen as a frequent but modest risk, has become a leading driver of insured losses in Europe and Canada, as the two organisations' remarks indicate, and that estimates for individual events can climb well beyond the first figure.
source_name: Reinsurance News (PERILS and CatIQ estimates, Oct 21, 2026)
image_alt: Hail-damaged vehicles and roofs representing severe convective storm losses (illustrative)
key_points: PERILS estimates insured losses from the severe convective storms of July 13 to 19, 2026, named SCS Cerry by the Free University of Berlin, at €2,806 million, up from an initial €2,186 million.
The event struck Germany, France, Switzerland and Italy, with some cells producing very large hail, damaging wind gusts and intense rainfall; the estimate covers property and motor lines.
The estimate is based on loss data from affected insurers, and a third estimate is due on January 19, 2027, six months after the event ended.
CatIQ, a PERILS subsidiary, raised its estimate for the September 2 and 3, 2026 severe convective storms in southern Ontario, including Toronto, to C$671 million from C$563 million.
Gallagher Re separately estimates European severe convective storm insured losses of at least $9 billion for the first nine months of 2026.
why_it_matters: Hailstorms are now one of the costliest weather risks for European insurers, and loss estimates tend to rise as claims are settled. The numbers help set the price of home and motor insurance and reinsurance in central Europe.

title: Hackers Sabotage Refrigeration Controllers at Hundreds of French Supermarkets, Raising Questions About Cyber Cover for Spoiled Food
summary: Attackers accessed internet-connected refrigeration controllers and triggered defrost cycles at stores run by Intermarché, Carrefour and Coopérative U in France, with about 700 stores reportedly disrupted according to Insurance Journal; no group has claimed responsibility.
description:
A cyberattack on French supermarkets has targeted something very different from customer data: the fridges. According to a report published by Insurance Journal on October 21, 2026, attackers accessed centralised, internet-connected refrigeration controllers, the systems that contractors use to monitor temperatures, and changed settings to trigger prolonged defrost cycles. The result was that fridges and freezers heated up, putting stocks of chilled and frozen food at risk across a large number of stores.

The report gives store counts rather than customer figures. Groupement Mousquetaires, the group that owns the Intermarché chain, said 300 of its stores were attacked. Carrefour said 80 supermarkets were affected. Coopérative U was also named as affected, though no separate count is given. The article says that the disruption hit 700 stores across Intermarché, Coopérative U and Carrefour. The date of the attack is not stated outright. The article refers to a store manager arriving "last Monday", and an accompanying photograph is dated October 12, 2026, so the incident probably occurred around that date.

Danfoss, a manufacturer whose equipment was affected, said most of the compromised devices were "obsolete models that no longer received software or security updates". That detail points to a common weakness. Industrial and building equipment is often installed for decades, may be connected to the internet for remote monitoring, and may not receive security patches once the manufacturer stops supporting it. No group has publicly claimed responsibility for the attack, so the motive is unknown. The sources reviewed do not say whether a ransom was demanded.

The financial impact on individual stores can be seen from one example. Store manager Jérémy Béziaud told the reporters that he threw out €3,000 ($3,370) of products. "I didn't want to take any risks since the cold chain had been broken," he said. The cold chain is the continuous refrigeration needed to keep food safe from production to sale, and food-safety rules typically require products that have been above safe temperatures for too long to be discarded. Multiplied across hundreds of stores, such losses could be significant, though the article does not provide an aggregate estimate.

An academic, Lallie of the University of Warwick, was quoted saying hackers are "targeting retail because they're weak and it can have a massive impact on society." The remark reflects a broader trend. Retailers hold large volumes of payment and personal data, operate on thin margins and rely on just-in-time supply chains, making disruption costly. An attack on refrigeration does not need to steal anything to create a loss.

The article carried no discussion of insurance, but the topic follows naturally. It links to another piece headlined "Insurers: French Supermarkets' Cyber Insurance Unlikely to Cover Food Losses". That article was not reviewed for this report, so its contents are not described here, but the headline captures a key issue. Standard cyber policies cover losses such as data restoration, ransom payments, business interruption caused by system failure and legal costs. Whether they cover physical damage to stock is less clear. Many cyber policies exclude or limit physical damage to tangible property, and many property policies exclude spoilage caused by cyber events or require that the cause be a specified peril such as power failure or equipment breakdown. Some policies offer "stock spoilage" or "contamination" extensions, and some add "cyber physical" cover, but the terms vary. The result is a potential gap between cyber and property insurance, which insurers refer to as "silent cyber" when coverage is unclear.

It is also worth separating what is known from what is not. The report establishes the method of attack, the equipment type, the companies that confirmed disruption and a sample loss from one store. It does not establish who carried out the attack, how long the disruption lasted, how many tonnes of food were discarded, whether any customers were affected or whether regulators have opened an investigation. The 700-store figure combines statements from different companies and the publication's own summary, and some stores may have been affected more severely than others. Until the companies publish fuller accounts, estimates of the total cost should be treated as speculation.

For the retailers, the practical lessons are to identify which operational technology devices are connected to the internet, to isolate them from corporate networks, to change default credentials, to replace unsupported equipment and to ensure that contractors' remote access is protected by strong authentication. Businesses should also check their insurance policies for how they treat spoilage caused by a cyber event, and talk to brokers about extensions. Food retailers might also consider backup temperature monitoring that does not rely on the same network.

For regulators and policymakers, the incident is another example of attackers moving from information technology to operational technology. A Google Cloud outage in London affected UK banks on October 20, illustrating a different type of dependency on shared technology. Both episodes show that essential services can be disrupted by a single point of failure or an insecure device.

For customers, the immediate effect appears limited to temporary stock losses and possible product shortages at affected stores; the article does not report food-safety incidents or recalls. It also does not report any data being exposed. Details such as the identity of the attackers, the full cost and the insurance response are not yet known, and further reporting is likely to clarify them. Readers should treat the store counts as company statements and the 700-store figure as the publication's summary.
image_alt: Supermarket refrigeration aisle representing a cold-chain cyber incident (illustrative)
key_points: Attackers accessed centralised, internet-connected fridge controllers that contractors use to monitor temperatures and changed settings to trigger prolonged defrost cycles.

Groupement Mousquetaires, which owns Intermarché, said 300 of its stores were attacked and Carrefour said 80 supermarkets were impacted; the article says the disruption hit about 700 stores across Intermarché, Coopérative U and Carrefour.
Danfoss, whose equipment was affected, said most compromised devices were obsolete models that no longer received software or security updates; no group has publicly claimed responsibility.

One store manager said he threw out €3,000 of products because the cold chain had been broken, and a University of Warwick expert said hackers target retail because it is weak and the impact on society can be large.
The article does not discuss insurance cover, data exposure or customer numbers; a linked headline suggests cyber policies are unlikely to cover food losses, but that article was not reviewed.
why_it_matters: This attack hit physical stock instead of stealing data, showing that cyber risk now reaches shop-floor equipment. It raises the question of whether cyber, property or stock spoilage insurance would pay when hackers cause food to spoil.

title: W. R. Berkley's Third-Quarter Premiums Rise to $3.95 Billion as the Specialty Insurer Posts a 90.8% Combined Ratio and Higher Investment Income
summary: W. R. Berkley reported Q3 2026 gross written premiums of $3.95 billion (up from $3.83 billion), a combined ratio of 90.8%, operating income of $456 million, net income of $446 million and net investment income of $383.5 million.
description:
W. R. Berkley, a US-based specialty property and casualty insurer, reported third-quarter 2026 results that show steady growth and strong profitability in a market where commercial prices are falling. According to Reinsurance News on October 20, 2026, the company's gross written premiums were $3.95 billion in the quarter, up from $3.83 billion a year earlier, which is growth of about 3%. For the first nine months of the year, gross written premiums reached $11.9 billion compared with $11.5 billion.

Most of the business is in the insurance segment, which had gross written premiums of $3.6 billion in the third quarter, up 4.9%, and $10.7 billion for the nine months, up 3.2%. The reinsurance segment is much smaller, with $391 million of gross written premiums in the quarter and $443 million for nine months. Net written premiums, the premiums retained after reinsurance, were $3.3 billion in the third quarter against $3.2 billion a year earlier, and $9.9 billion for nine months versus $9.7 billion. Net premiums earned, the amount recognised as revenue in the period, were $3.21 billion compared with $3.15 billion, and $9.5 billion for nine months versus $9.3 billion.

Underwriting performance remained strong. The reported combined ratio, which compares claims and expenses with premiums, was 90.8%, meaning about nine cents of every premium dollar was left as underwriting profit before investment income. The current accident year combined ratio excluding catastrophe losses, a measure of the underlying performance of the year's business without weather events, was 88.1%. The insurance segment's pre-tax underwriting income rose 10.6% to $237.7 million. The article does not give reserve development or rate changes by segment, so it is not possible to say how much of the result came from favourable prior-year reserves or how much prices are moving.

Catastrophe losses were modest. They were $85.9 million in the third quarter, up from $78.5 million a year earlier, and $223 million for the nine months, down from $288 million. The decline in the nine-month figure is consistent with the broader market: Gallagher Re estimates global insured natural-catastrophe losses for the first nine months of 2026 at $92 billion, the lowest since 2019 and 29% below the ten-year average.

Profit figures show a mixed picture. Net income fell to $446 million in the third quarter from $511 million a year earlier, although for nine months it rose to $1.4 billion from $1.3 billion. Operating income, which excludes items such as investment gains and losses, rose to $456 million from $440 million in the quarter, and to $1.5 billion from $1.3 billion for the nine months. The article describes the quarterly operating income increase as 6.4%, but the two dollar figures given imply an increase of about 3.6%; the percentage may reflect unrounded figures, and readers should check the company's release for the precise number. The drop in net income despite higher operating income is likely to reflect the timing of investment gains and other non-operating items, though the article does not explain it.

Investment income continued to grow. Net investment income was $383.5 million in the quarter compared with $351 million a year earlier, an increase of about 9%. The article labels the quarter as "Q2'26", which appears to be a typographical error. For nine months, investment income was $1.2 billion compared with $1 billion. The article attributes the growth to a 12% increase in the core portfolio, meaning the insurer has more assets to invest, in addition to the yields available.

W. Robert Berkley, Jr., the company's chairman and chief executive, said the company generated "an annualized 18.8% operating return on beginning-of-year stockholders' equity." On underwriting, he said: "Our underwriting results have consistently been outstanding." Return on equity of that size is high for an insurer, and it indicates how profitable the specialty business has been, though it is the company's own measure.

Context matters. Berkley's niche markets, including excess and surplus lines, professional liability and other specialty lines, benefited from the hard market that began in 2019 and extended through 2023. Now, Marsh reports that global commercial rates fell about 5% in the third quarter, the ninth consecutive decline, and CRC Group says US property renewals are down roughly 11%, though casualty rates in the US are still rising, by 6% according to Marsh. Chubb's chief executive has warned about "hungry and extremely naive capacity." Against that backdrop, Berkley's growth of about 3% in premiums and a combined ratio of 90.8% indicate a company that is growing selectively. The article does not say whether the company is writing less business in areas where prices have fallen.

What should investors and customers take from this? For investors, the key questions are whether Berkley can keep a combined ratio near 90% as pricing softens, and how much future earnings depend on investment income. For customers, a financially strong specialty insurer can offer capacity for hard-to-place risks, though prices and terms will depend on the line. For the market, the results are another sign that insurers remain profitable, and that the debate is about how long conditions last.

Several details were not covered by the article: the share count and per-share earnings, the book value, share repurchases, reserve development and the breakdown of premium growth by line of business. Readers who need those should consult the company's earnings release.
source_name: Reinsurance News (W. R. Berkley Q3 2026 results, October 20, 2026)

key_points: W. R. Berkley's gross written premiums were $3.95 billion in Q3 2026, up from $3.83 billion, and $11.9 billion for nine months versus $11.5 billion.
The reported combined ratio was 90.8% and the current accident year combined ratio excluding catastrophe losses was 88.1%; insurance segment pre-tax underwriting income rose 10.6% to $237.7 million.
Net income fell to $446 million from $511 million in the quarter, while operating income rose to $456 million from $440 million.
Catastrophe losses were $85.9 million in the quarter versus $78.5 million, and $223 million for nine months versus $288 million.
Net investment income rose to $383.5 million from $351 million, and the chairman said the company generated an annualised 18.8% operating return on beginning-of-year equity.
why_it_matters: Berkley is a leading specialty and excess-and-surplus insurer, so its numbers show how a disciplined niche underwriter is doing while broad commercial prices fall. Modest growth with a combined ratio near 90% suggests profitability remains good but the easy growth of the hard market is over.
